title: How Do You Take a Picture of a Black Hole?
content:
Black holes are one of the universe’s most exotic and elusive objects. When nothing, not even light, can escape their powerful gravitational grasp, taking a picture of one seems unimaginable. But an image of a black hole, or more accurately its shadow, could offer insights that theory alone may not provide when testing predictions. So how can it be done?

Harvard astrophysicist Shep Doeleman and a team of 250 researchers achieved this extraordinary feat by linking a group of radio telescopes around the world. This network, called the Event Horizon Telescope, produced the first image of a supermassive black hole in the galaxy M87, around 55 million light-years away, and the first image of the black hole at the heart of our galaxy. In this episode, Doeleman tells co-host Janna Levin how he turned the Earth into a telescope capable of seeing a black hole, the incredible level of science and collaboration that was required to achieve this, how the images have furthered our understanding of these exotic objects, and how movies of black holes may be possible by the early 2030s.

Listen on [Apple Podcasts (opens a new tab)](https://podcasts.apple.com/us/podcast/the-joy-of-why/id1608948873), [Spotify (opens a new tab)](https://open.spotify.com/show/2FoxHraQSKwxV2HgUfwLMp), [TuneIn (opens a new tab)](https://tunein.com/podcasts/Science-Podcasts/The-Joy-of-Why-p1653040/) or your favorite podcasting app, or you can [stream it from Quanta](https://www.quantamagazine.org/tag/the-joy-of-why).

## **Transcript**

**JANNA LEVIN:** Okay. I’m Janna Levin

**STEVE STROGATZ:** And I’m Steve Strogatz.

**LEVIN:** And this is _The Joy of Why_

**STROGATZ:** A podcast from _Quanta Magazine_ where we look at some of the biggest unanswered questions in math and science today.

**LEVIN:** Welcome to another episode.

**STROGATZ:** Great to see you.

**LEVIN:** Great to see you. I’m pretty excited about this one. I cannot deny or hide it. We’re talking about not only an area where I’ve spent a lot of my life black holes — the greatest, strangest topic out there — but also I had a chance to talk to an old friend. So it’s a fun episode, I hope.

**STROGATZ:** I’m really looking forward to hearing it. I know you’ve always had a special affection for black holes. I’ve had a chance to interview you in some earlier version of this.

**LEVIN:** That’s right.

**STROGATZ:** And you blew my mind over and over about black holes.

**LEVIN:** Yeah, they require some defense. They’ve got a bad reputation, not entirely earned.

**STROGATZ:** What’s the bad reputation? Because they like to eat things?

**LEVIN:** Yeah. You know, black holes, kind of this monster truck language around black holes all the time. You know, they’re like… But actually, black holes are remarkably elegant, clean, simple systems. They leave you alone if you leave them alone. They’re actually quite small for their heft. That’s kind of their whole gestalt, that they’re actually tiny for their heft.

And, uh, you know, though they’re the darkest phenomenon in the universe, they figure out a way to become the brightest beacons that we see on the edge of what’s observable.

**STROGATZ:** Wow.

**LEVIN:** So, they’re, they’re pretty awesome. I also think that they’re fundamental to physics, unlike any other macroscopic object you can think of.

**STROGATZ:** Hmmm. When I think of black holes, I tend to focus on what they do to spacetime. You know, that they cause singularities. It’s their geometry that always grabs me. But that’s not really necessarily the only way to think about black holes. They’re really objects. Real players.

**LEVIN:** Yeah. I think after people got over the thrill that they actually existed out there and that they could indirectly be detected, there was a sense that they’re not major players in the universe. “Eh, so there’s some black holes out there.”

Quite to the contrary, I think we’ve come to understand that they sculpt our history and our past, that they have a very regulating and important role in determining the shape and size of galaxies and where there might be habitable regions even. And ultimately, we’re kinda doomed to fall into black holes eventually. So, they’re kind of our past and our future.

But, it might surprise people that we had never actually taken a picture of a black hole. All of our evidence had been indirect until about 10 years ago, and that group worked for well over a decade, for some people up to two decades, to try to capture the first picture of a black hole.

**STROGATZ:** Huh. Wild.

**LEVIN:** It was a tremendous accomplishment, led by Shep Doeleman, who is our guest. So let me tell you about Shep. Shep is a senior research fellow at Harvard University, the assistant director of Harvard’s Black Hole Initiative, also an astrophysicist at the Smithsonian Astrophysical Observatory.

And he was the founding director of the Event Horizon Telescope Consortium, which is a network of observatories around the world which gave us the first and only images humanity has ever captured of black holes.

**STROGATZ:** Hmm. This sounds like it’s gonna be a great discussion of science at its best.

**LEVIN:** Yeah, it’s an epic story. Let’s hear from Shep himself.

[_Music plays_]

**LEVIN:** Shep, welcome to _The Joy of Why_.

**SHEP DOELEMAN:** It’s good to be here, Janna.

**LEVIN:** It’s a pleasure to have you on the show. I’m really curious if you remember not just your way into black holes, but your way into the entire idea of thinking about the universe?

**DOELEMAN:** Wow. Well, everybody falls in love with astronomy at some point. I don’t care who you are, you fall in love with astronomy. And whether it’s staring up at the night sky, you know, at summer camp or seeing a meteorite, for me, it was seeing a total solar eclipse. I was 13, 1980. And my parents took me out to the middle of the desert in Oregon and at first we thought we weren’t gonna see totality, the clouds were moving in, and then the clouds just parted and we saw this amazing eclipse. It was just tremendous.

**LEVIN:** Did you think at that moment, “Well, this is what I’m gonna do for the rest of my life”? Or is it that the memory comes back and we reconstruct the story, you know?

**DOELEMAN:** That’s a great question. I think it mostly, it just comes back. Life isn’t linear like that. But I will say the idea that there would be these huge objects that were moving and they could align perfectly and allow you to see what would normally be hidden, like the corona of the sun, was startling to me. I mean, it didn’t have to be that way. Like, the angular diameter of the moon doesn’t have to be the same as the sun so they totally block each other out. But these coincidences sometimes give you a special view into nature.

**LEVIN:** Yeah. I, I love that there’s just this idea that we’re inspired by the firmament, science’s oldest instrument, and that we all have it in common.

Um, so I really feel we have to make a confession ’cause we’ve known each other a really long time. I feel like we met maybe the first week of graduate school at MIT. I think over a cookie table.

**DOELEMAN:**I think so.

**LEVIN:**So I remember just you were always trying these crazy ideas in graduate school. You were like a creative curiosity in search of a problem. Tell me a little bit first about how you landed on this idea of pursuing a portrait of a black hole?

**DOELEMAN:** Portrait of a black hole, I love that. So I graduated high school pretty early. I was 15 years old. And went to college, and then after that I was pretty burned out, and I saw an advertisement that said, “Go to Antarctica and run all these experiments down there.” And I said, “That’s for me.” I interviewed for the position, and somehow they gave it to this 19-year-old kid. They needed some warm body down there to look after the cosmic ray experiments, the aerophotometry experiments, the electromagnetic experiments, and I got a real taste for doing experimental research in difficult circumstances. I just loved it. And then came back to MIT, where I met you in 1988.

**LEVIN:** Oh, you didn’t have to say the year, man. That was unnecessary [_laughs_].

**DOELEMAN:** I know, when the Earth was cooling. But, I cast around a bit. I started in the X-ray group there, and then I did a little bit of neuroscience looking at biophysics. And then I was introduced to this idea of turning the Earth into a telescope, and this experiment that we use to image black holes and that immediately drew me in.

**LEVIN:** Yeah. So we’re gonna talk about this project, but when you were in graduate school, what was the status of black holes scientifically? Were they detected? Did everyone believe that they were real astrophysical phenomena?

**DOELEMAN:** There was really a sense that black holes existed or strong evidence for them. And of course, there are two flavors of black holes. There are stellar-mass black holes which form during star death. So when a star goes supernova, it will explode the outer shells off, and then the interior part will collapse and if the star is massive enough, it will turn into a black hole, and that black hole could be tens of solar masses.

But then there are these behemoths, these supermassive black holes that live in the centers of galaxies. And while there can be many stellar-mass black holes in a galaxy, there’s probably just one, maybe two, supermassive black holes at the core of any given galaxy.

And for the stellar-mass black holes, people had seen these X-ray binaries, and they were seeing very fast fluctuations in X-rays and even in the radio from these stellar-sized sources. And everything fit with this idea that there was a black hole eating another star that goes an X-ray binary.

**LEVIN:** And that was Cygnus X-1, a first X-ray object in the direction of the constellation Cygnus, right?

**DOELEMAN:** Exactly, it was those kinds of sources. And then the radio people predominantly had seen some very high-resolution images that were very troubling. So you would see in the optical, a galaxy would look like a normal run-of-the-mill galaxy with a lot of optical light coming from stars.

But then if you looked at it in the radio, you would see these oppositely directed jets of material all tracing to the center of the galaxy. What is causing that?

And the best idea that people had for that was a spinning supermassive black hole that was energizing jets that moved at near light speed from the north and south pole of that black hole, and it was piercing the entire galaxy.

So from two completely different lines of inquiry you had one flavor of black holes being suspected from the X-ray, and you had another suspected predominantly by the radio.

**LEVIN:** So even though people started to theorize that these must be black holes, nobody had taken a picture of a black hole, not in the ’70s, ’80s, ’90s, the noughts. I think that was a surprise to people because we talked about them as being such compelling inhabitants of the universe, death states of stars, but we had actually technically never seen one directly. Never taken a portrait. And that’s really what you set out to do in many ways.

**DOELEMAN:** Yeah. I think the simplest way of saying it is that seeing is believing in a certain way. I mean, you can theorize something, but actually seeing it confers a reality on things that you don’t get otherwise. And there were some really important signatures, too. It wasn’t just seeing it. It was measuring it. Taking the measure of the thing not only gives you confidence in its reality, but you can test predictions.

So in 1915, when Einstein came with his theory of general relativity, which governs the space time around a black hole, and then the year after that Schwarzschild solved it in the trenches of World War I, a story that we know well, even after that, it was pretty clear that if you went to the conclusion of that solution, you would wind up seeing a ring of light around the black hole.

That if a bunch of gas was drawn to the black hole, it heated up to hundreds of billions of degrees because you’re confining it to a small volume, and it emits light. That light would be curved by the gravitational force of the black hole. And from any direction that you look at the black hole, you would see a ring of light. Basically, the emission from behind the black hole lensed around into a ring. And the size of that ring you can derive from Einstein’s equations.

And so we theorized that if we could make a photo, if we could see this ring, we’d be able to measure the mass of the black hole. But also just the ring itself would be like the best evidence for the existence of supermassive black holes at that scale. So it wasn’t just a coffee table book we were after. We were after the real measurement of the fundamental nature of the universe.

**LEVIN:** Now, when people hear this idea that you’re gonna try to turn the Earth into a telescope or a telescope the size of the world, it sounds like such a crazy lark. What made you think it was viable? It was no mean feat.

**DOELEMAN:** Yeah. Well, so, so this idea of turning the Earth into a telescope had been around for a long time, since the ‘60s. And the key is that the angular resolution of a telescope or the ability to magnify things on the sky, it scales as the wavelength of light you’re observing, lambda, divided by the size of your telescope.

So if you wanna see things that are really small in the sky, you either reduce your wavelength of light or you expand the size of your telescope. So you’ll often see these huge blocks of glass on top of mountaintops. These huge optical dishes, and they’re big for a reason. They collect a lot of light, but also the bigger they are, the smaller the objects they can see.

**LEVIN:** The better the resolution.

**DOELEMAN:** The better the resolution, precisely. And so there are some objects that are so small, and black holes are the smallest objects predicted by Einstein’s theory of gravity, that you need extremely big telescopes, extremely fine angular resolution to see them, and you’ve gotta take this idea of turning the Earth into a telescope to the utmost extremes.

You have to operate it at wavelengths that had never been operated before ’cause you have to really go to smaller and smaller wavelengths to get the angular resolution you need. And that’s what took us 20 years, to push the technique to the absolute limit.

**LEVIN:** Yeah. So there’s a couple of things. One is a lot of people are surprised to hear that black holes are small. They imagine that they’re enormous. Can you explain that to us? Why they’re actually spatially tiny even though they’re incredibly hefty?

**DOELEMAN:** Yeah. Black holes simply put are when you confine enough matter into a small enough volume that the force of gravity runs away and the material undergoes catastrophic gravitational collapse into a point of infinite density. And you’d think, “Okay, that’s pretty tiny,” but what happens is that around that is a membrane called the event horizon, and that’s where the gravitational force is so strong that light can’t escape. So that really defines the region of space that we can observe ourselves.

And then astrophysical black holes are not invisible, because you would think to yourself, “Well, if you can’t see it,” because it’s got this event horizon around it, but they attract gas and dust and everything you can imagine to them, and you’re cramming it all into a very, very small space so it heats up. And so in a paradox of their own gravity, these black holes can shine extremely brightly.

And if you get one that’s at the center of a galaxy that weighs millions or billions of times what our sun does, it can outshine all the combined light of the stars in that galaxy. So you see these very small objects, but they can be extremely bright.

**LEVIN:** So how did they deduce that that’s a black hole if that wasn’t predicted, if that wasn’t expected?

**DOELEMAN:** Yeah, a lot of it was the timescale of the variations because that tells you the scale of what you’re looking at. So typically in astronomy, if you see something that is varying on a certain timescale, you just say, “Well, I think it can move faster than the speed of light.” And so this gives you an idea of how big that object can be.

And for its luminosity, it was very difficult to think that there could be anything bigger than a black hole that was causing these kinds of fluctuations. And then there was the amount of energy coming out was related to it falling into this gravitational well and energy being liberated. That was another clue that people had. So as you say, there were these indirect methods of modeling what we were seeing as black holes, and the black holes fit the best.

For the supermassive black holes, there people could see the energy coming out of these jets, and really the only mechanism that we could think of was magnetic fields twisting in the warped space time of the black hole itself. And like egg beaters twisting around, they fling these charged particles out at near the speed of light. And the observations were so extreme that really that’s the only model that fit. And miraculously, as you got better and better angular resolution, as you trace the jet all the way down to the center, it kept looking like this jet.

It didn’t break this model. You kept seeing this jet getting closer and closer and closer, and there was this mad idea that we had to see what was causing this.

**LEVIN:** So let’s distinguish death states of stars, which are the kinds of objects that were creating signals like Cygnus X-1. Two star systems born and died together. One becomes a black hole, the other starts to descend. It gets cannibalized. It creates these X-rays, these jets. These supermassive black holes, at the time we were calling them quasi-stellar objects or quasars, right? It was not understood where these supermassive black holes came from or if they were so prevalent, if they had permeated the entire universe. I mean, it was a surprise, wasn’t it, that those quasars were commonplace, that they probably exist in every single galaxy.

**DOELEMAN:** Yeah. There’s a lot of different lines of evidence for this. Certainly for the galaxies that are radio loud and where you can do interferometry along the lines of what we did to take the picture of the black hole. There, you wind up seeing these jets of material, and those account for maybe 10% of the galaxies that we see. For the other galaxies, we see these cusps of stellar population that increase dramatically as you get to the center, and so you can postulate that there could be a supermassive black hole there.

And now with better resolution and better telescopes, we’ve seen the statistical velocities of stars very, very close to the center of these galaxies within a couple of light years of these galaxies. And it’s now become clear that all galaxies seem to have these super massive black holes at their cores.

And why some are radio loud, why some emit in the radio waves, why some don’t probably has a lot to do with the direction that you’re looking at them. It also has to do with the evolutionary moment in the lifespan of that galaxy. Some radio loud at some times and some not at other times. So we’re seeing the great variety, like the zoo of galaxies across cosmic time, and we’re fortunate that some of them really exhibit these tremendously illuminating radio structures that we can image with an Earth-sized telescope.

And that’s really what drove the field of radio interferometry. We needed to make a picture that was, let’s say, 10,000 times better than anything that we had made before. And the magic of interferometry is that you can detect radio waves from a black hole, let’s say in Chile, and you can time tag them with an atomic clock so you see all the crests and the troughs of these radio waves as they’re coming in. And you can do the same thing in, let’s say Hawai‘i. And then you can bring those waveforms together and compare them as though they had been received by one huge telescope, and they will be coherent. You can play them back against each other, and you can line up the troughs and the crests. Now this is the secret that allows you to turn the Earth into a telescope.

**LEVIN:** So this is what you mean when you say very long baseline interferometry or interferometry in general. You’re talking about connecting these dishes around the globe. Now, it’s over decades that this work really begins in imagination, conception, execution. But, when was the Event Horizon Telescope as a project officially founded?

**DOELEMAN:** Well, it depends. I’d wrote my thesis in 1995 and pushed the technique up to wavelengths that were close but not quite sufficient to do this black hole imaging. So we had a pretty good idea of where we were going. And then we really started in earnest thinking about it in maybe 1998. We started doing experiments that were gonna push it to these frontier frequencies, like 230 gigahertz, that were high enough that it would be able to see through all the gas and dust.

In 2008, we discovered event horizon scale structure in the galactic center. And then, I wrote a paper along with a small number of colleagues for the 2010 Decadal Review, in which we said we’re building an event horizon telescope in the next decade. So that’s when I kinda think we kicked things off. The actual Event Horizon Telescope formed as a body in 2016, and I was the founding director of that.

**LEVIN:** So, where were the telescopes originally that you were using?

**DOELEMAN:** Well, let’s see. South Pole, there were two telescopes in Chile, a telescope in Mexico, two telescopes in Hawai‘i, telescope in Arizona — two telescopes now in Arizona. One in Spain, one in France, and that was just enough.

**LEVIN:** You know, what’s so fascinating about this project, was that all of these telescopes existed. The idea was to use telescopes that already existed that were being used for other purposes, not the same idea at all as building a satellite and starting from scratch.

How did that go over, this idea of trying to build a coalition out of all of these different observatories? And, it’s a really international collaboration. I mean, hundreds of people.

**DOELEMAN:** I’ll, I’ll put it to you this way. In my group, we spent a lot of time working on instrumentation that would allow a telescope to record information that could then be compared to recordings made at other telescopes. This is how interferometry works on a global scale.

But this was not what these telescopes were doing, so we had to convince these telescopes that we could bring our instrumentation, bolt it in, in some cases manhandle some of their very, very sensitive equipment, operate the telescope in a way that it had not been designed to be operated in, and then take all these disks with data and disappear, and then maybe tell them months later what happened.

And that’s the key thing because we needed to get time on these telescopes, and we had to convince them that this was a worthy project. And we had done enough precursor observations, and we detected event horizon-scale structure in the galactic center in the Milky Way black hole, this is the four million solar mass black hole at the center of our Milky Way galaxy. We detected that, and so they were listening to us, but they were still kinda skeptical that we were gonna be able to pull this off. And it was a lot of cajoling. There was a lot of convincing. There was a lot of applying for time. But we were careful, and we produced results all along the way. And then people began to realize you might actually pull this off. And so they kinda let us in. They gave us the keys to the observatory…

**LEVIN:** Uh-huh.

**DOELEMAN:** … Like “Have it back by midnight.” You know, that kind of thing.

**LEVIN:** Right. I also wanna return to the idea of the atomic clock, because these atomic clocks are so precise that, what you lose a few seconds over the age of the universe?

**DOELEMAN:** Uh, well, no, they’re not, they’re not that good. And I’ve been around for most of the age of the universe, so I know. So yeah, so the key thing is that when you record the radio waves at any of the Event Horizon Telescope sites, you need for the signal not to jitter.

It has to be stable so that when you have another one, they line up in just the right way. And if the signal is jittering back and forth because your clock is imperfect, you’ll never be able to line up these waveforms from different parts of the Earth.

So you need a super stable clock. We use hydrogen maser clocks, and these lose about one second every 10 million years or so, and that’s the stability that we need in order to keep everything stable.

**LEVIN:** I see.

**DOELEMAN:** I remember being at the Large Millimeter Telescope in Mexico and watching as they winched one of these atomic clocks up the central part of a helical staircase, and just like wondering what I was doing at 15,000 feet watching this precision timepiece being winched up and into place.

And then we put it into a wooden enclosure because, you know, it needed to be at a certain temperature, and we used light bulbs inside to heat it to just the right temperature. So you get very imaginative when you’re at the top of a mountain, how am I gonna keep this atomic clock you know, swaddled?

**LEVIN:** Right. And you still need for nature to comply, ’cause you need the weather to go your way. You can’t have snow accumulating in the telescope. It can’t freeze if you’re trying to point it. And so there is genuinely a lot of that in making an observation.

**DOELEMAN:** Well, so every evening before we trigger the observations, we have to make sure that the weather is good everywhere.

**LEVIN:** Now, when you’re stringing all these instruments together and you have these incredibly precise atomic clocks, and so you’re lining up the crest so you’re now have one big eye taking in these objects that looking in a certain direction and focusing on a particular object, how good a resolution have you gotten?

**DOELEMAN:** So for example, the supermassive black hole in the center of the Milky Way galaxy is 4 million times the mass of the sun. At the distance of the center of the galaxy, about 27,000 light years, the whole lensed part of the event horizon subtends about 50 microarcseconds.

Now, that’s insanely small. That’s like, you know, if you’re in New York City and your friend is holding a quarter in Los Angeles, you can read the date on that quarter. Or if there’s a tangerine or really a citrus fruit of any variety on the moon, you could see that fruit. Even a pomelo, possibly a tangerine.

**LEVIN:** Let’s not be picky.

**DOELEMAN:** And, so we’re, we’re trying to get the highest angular resolution possible from the surface of our planet. That’s what’s needed.

**LEVIN:** So when we’re talking about these black holes, even the one that’s closest to us, which you just mentioned at 27,000 light years away in the center of our own Milky Way galaxy, is barely, barely on the edge of visibility. What other supermassive black holes could we possibly see?

**DOELEMAN:** Well, so we’re lucky in the sense that we have one, Sagittarius A*, that we felt for sure we could image. And then there was another one, M87, which is in the constellation Virgo. That black hole is about six billion times what our sun weighs, but it’s fifty-five million light years away. So it’s about two thousand times farther away, but it’s also about two thousand times more massive. And the event horizon scales with mass, so its angular size is about the same as the supermassive black hole in the center of the Milky Way galaxy.

**LEVIN:** Now, I remember when you sent me a note saying there’s going to be a press conference. So I come racing out to the National Press Club in Washington, DC ’cause I know you’re not holding a press conference to tell us you failed. So here is the moment, where you’re about to reveal the first picture humanity has ever procured of a black hole ever. And I’m expecting what we call Sagittarius A*, our own black hole in the center of the Milky Way that we’ve been discussing. But instead it’s M87. I did not expect this. Were you surprised that that’s what you were able to resolve first? Did you know people like me would be surprised?

**DOELEMAN:** You know, it all makes sense when you look back on it. Of course, Sagittarius A* was the preferred candidate. We’re all in love with our own supermassive black hole in the center of the Milky Way galaxy.

But there’s a problem with Sagittarius A* as much as we love it, because it’s only 4 million solar masses, the time it takes matter to orbit Sagittarius A* is only about half an hour. Now, what that means is that during a night of observing, the thing you’re trying to take an image of is changing in its appearance. Things are orbiting around it, it’s burbling, it’s turbulent, and it looks different from one moment to the next. In aggregate, averaged, you would see this ring, but from moment to moment it would change.

So even from first principles, we should have realized that imaging that source would’ve been much more difficult, whereas M87*, is 6 billion solar masses, so the timescales scale with mass. So during a night of observing, it’s essentially stationary. It’s not changing its appearance at all, so you can add up all the data you take during a night of observing with all the changing look directions and the changing baselines as the Earth is turning to build up a very, very good image. So, that’s the one we came with first because it was much easier to image. But being able to announce that discovery, and knowing that there was astronomers who were experts who were taken by surprise, that was actually kind of cool about the whole thing.

**LEVIN:** [_Laughs_] Yeah.

**DOELEMAN:** We finally did come with an image of Sag A*, but only after we had overcome the algorithmic problems of how to deal with something that’s changing while you’re looking at it. So we have two of these sources, and we’ve imaged both of them with the Event Horizon Telescope.

And when we laid a ruler across the spacetime of the event horizon, we did verify that for their mass, they’re exactly the size that Einstein predicted, to within the uncertainty of our measurements, which is the best evidence that we have for the existence of supermassive black holes in the centers of galaxies. And also, yay for Einstein. He keeps passing all these tests that we throw at him.

[_Music plays_]

**STROGATZ:** It’s very inspiring to listen to the story of how much science goes in to make the stunning image that a billion people or whatever got to see. How much fundamental science between the atomic clocks, the idea of interferometers, all the general relativity…

**LEVIN:** I totally agree that this remarkable precision of the clock that they needed, and the industriousness of being on the edge of observability, I mean, it really was almost impossible. You could totally have imagined that somebody would’ve said, “This is ridiculous. Give this up. You need a telescope the size of the Earth, so move on to something else. We’ll never see a picture of any black hole ever.”

And instead, they thought, “Well, how would I make a telescope the size of the Earth,” and calling on observatories that had been in use for other purposes, as opposed to building a fundamentally new instrument.

So I just loved so much that went into it: the preexisting observatories, the notions of the timing having become so precise and linking it together just on the edge of observability. Really, it’s just a few pixels that they have.

**STROGATZ:** You raise an interesting point about existing observatories. I hadn’t appreciated that, that unlike LIGO, Ray Weiss and that vision where you had to create a whole new instrument to get the gravitational wave detection, in this case, the observatories existed, but the ingenuity seems to be the coordination.
